Hydrocarbons.intro: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that is separated by fractional distillation.

sections.title: Crude Oil
points: Formed from ancient marine organisms over millions of years — non-renewable fossil fuel
Mixture of many different hydrocarbons
Separated by fractional distillation based on boiling point

sections.title: Fractional Distillation
points: Crude oil heated and vaporised; vapours rise up a fractionating column
Column is cooler at the top — temperature gradient
Fractions condense at different levels depending on boiling point
Smaller molecules: lower boiling point, more flammable, less viscous, more volatile
Larger molecules: higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable
Fractions (top to bottom): gases, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen

keyTerms.def: A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen
A mixture of hydrocarbons formed from ancient organisms — a fossil fuel
Separation of a mixture based on different boiling points
A group of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points collected at one level

examTips: Shorter carbon chains = lower boiling point = more flammable = less viscous.
Fractional distillation is a PHYSICAL separation — no new substances formed.
commonMistakes: Confusing fractional distillation (physical) with cracking (chemical decomposition).
Saying lighter fractions have higher boiling points — it's the opposite.

Alkanes.intro: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons — they contain only single C-C bonds. They are the main components of crude oil fractions.

sections.title: Alkane Structure
points: General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Only single C-C bonds — SATURATED
Methane CH₄, Ethane C₂H₆, Propane C₃H₈, Butane C₄H₁₀

sections.title: Combustion of Alkanes
points: Complete combustion (excess O₂): hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (blue flame)
Incomplete combustion (limited O₂): produces CO (toxic) and carbon (soot)
Carbon monoxide is toxic — binds to haemoglobin, preventing O₂ transport

keyTerms.def: Saturated hydrocarbon with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Contains only single C-C bonds — no double bonds
Burning in excess oxygen → CO₂ and H₂O
Burning in limited oxygen → CO and carbon (soot)

examTips: Complete combustion = CO₂ + H₂O (clean). Incomplete = CO + C (dirty, toxic).
Alkanes are saturated — do NOT decolourise bromine water.
commonMistakes: Saying incomplete combustion produces CO₂ — it produces CO (carbon monoxide).

Alkenes.intro: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a C=C double bond. They are more reactive than alkanes and used to make polymers.

sections.title: Alkene Structure
points: General formula: CₙH₂ₙ
Contain one C=C double bond — UNSATURATED
Ethene C₂H₄, Propene C₃H₆, Butene C₄H₈

callout.label: Bromine Water Test
callout.text: Add bromine water (orange). Alkene present → decolourises to colourless. Alkane → no change (stays orange).

sections.title: Addition Reactions
points: The C=C double bond opens up — atoms add across it
Hydrogenation: alkene + H₂ → alkane (nickel catalyst, 150°C)
Hydration: alkene + H₂O → alcohol (steam, phosphoric acid catalyst)
Halogenation: alkene + Br₂ → dibromoalkane (this decolourises bromine water)

keyTerms.def: Unsaturated hydrocarbon with C=C double bond; formula CₙH₂ₙ
Contains at least one C=C double bond
Atoms add across a C=C double bond — only one product formed

examTips: Bromine water test: alkenes decolourise it (orange → colourless); alkanes do not.
Addition reactions have 100% atom economy — all atoms end up in the product.
commonMistakes: Saying alkanes decolourise bromine water — only alkenes do this.
Forgetting that addition reactions produce only ONE product.

Cracking.intro: Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones. It is essential because demand for shorter-chain fractions exceeds supply.

sections.title: Why Crack?
points: Crude oil contains too many long-chain fractions (not enough petrol, diesel)
Cracking converts surplus long chains into shorter, more useful ones
Also produces alkenes — essential for making polymers

sections.title: Types of Cracking
points: Thermal cracking: 700°C+, high pressure — mainly alkenes produced
Catalytic cracking: lower temperature (~500°C), aluminium oxide catalyst — mainly petrol and alkenes

callout.label: Example
callout.text: Decane (C₁₀H₂₂) → octane (C₈H₁₈) + ethene (C₂H₄). Always produces at least one alkene.

keyTerms.def: Breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller ones using heat (and sometimes a catalyst)
Cracking using aluminium oxide catalyst at ~500°C
Cracking using high temperature (700°C+) and pressure

examTips: Cracking always produces at least one alkene — important for polymer production.
Cracking is thermal decomposition — it needs heat and sometimes a catalyst.
commonMistakes: Saying cracking only produces alkanes — it always produces alkenes too.
Confusing cracking (chemical change) with fractional distillation (physical separation).

Polymers.intro: Polymers are very long chain molecules formed by joining many small monomer units together. Plastics are synthetic polymers.

sections.title: Addition Polymerisation
points: Unsaturated monomers (with C=C) join together
C=C double bond opens up, monomers join in a long chain
Only ONE product — 100% atom economy
Examples: ethene → poly(ethene); propene → poly(propene)

callout.label: Naming Rule
callout.text: Put 'poly' in front of the monomer name in brackets. E.g. ethene → poly(ethene). Propene → poly(propene).

sections.title: Issues with Plastics
points: Non-biodegradable — persist in environment for centuries
Microplastics enter food chains
Solutions: recycling, biodegradable plastics, reducing plastic use

keyTerms.def: A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units joined together
A small molecule that joins with others to form a polymer
Monomers with C=C bonds join together — no other products

examTips: Monomers need C=C bonds for addition polymerisation.
Name polymer by putting 'poly' before monomer name in brackets.
commonMistakes: Using alkanes as monomers — need alkenes (C=C double bonds).
Forgetting the brackets in polymer names — poly(ethene) not polyethene.

Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids.intro: Alcohols and carboxylic acids are important functional group families. Ethanol and ethanoic acid are the key examples.

sections.title: Alcohols
points: Functional group: -OH
General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
Methanol CH₃OH, Ethanol C₂H₅OH, Propanol C₃H₇OH
Soluble in water; used as fuels and solvents
Ethanol made by: fermentation (glucose + yeast → ethanol + CO₂) or hydration of ethene

sections.title: Carboxylic Acids
points: Functional group: -COOH
Ethanoic acid CH₃COOH — found in vinegar
Weakly acidic — partially ionise in water
React with alcohols to form esters + water (esterification)
Esters have characteristic fruity smells — used in perfumes and flavourings

keyTerms.def: Organic compound containing an -OH functional group
Organic compound containing a -COOH functional group
Compound formed from alcohol + carboxylic acid — fruity smell
Anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast producing ethanol and CO₂

examTips: Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water
Ethanoic acid is a WEAK acid — do not confuse with strong acids like HCl.
commonMistakes: Saying fermentation uses oxygen — it is an ANAEROBIC process.
